content.title: About
content.content: Chickpeas (Cicer arietinum) are a legume native to the Mediterranean, South Asia and North Africa. The seeds have a nutty flavor, firm texture and are used whole, as flour, in hummus and in a wide range of dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chickpeas belong to the legume family and have been cultivated for over 7,000 years.
In India they are called “garbanzo” or “chana”, while in the Mediterranean they are often referred to as “Egyptian peas”.
The plant can fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil.
Chickpeas are a staple in vegetarian and vegan diets as a plant‑based protein source.
More than 50 varieties exist, differing in size, color and flavor.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Chickpeas provide about 20 % protein, making them a valuable amino‑acid source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of iron and folate
items.content: Iron aids oxygen transport, while folate is essential for cell division and fetal development.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals contribute to muscle function, nerve health and bone formation.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Chickpeas raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for diabetes management.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chickpeas, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting helps mitigate this.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Legumes can cause increased gas in sensitive people.

items.title: Potential gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: People with celiac disease should choose certified gluten‑free chickpeas.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chickpeas can be boiled, roasted, baked, ground into flour, or blended into hummus. Add them to salads, soups, stews, curries, as well as to vegetarian patties and falafel.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry chickpeas in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage keep them in the refrigerator. Cooked chickpeas keep in the fridge for 4‑5 days.
